title: Selective and High Current CO2 Electro-Reduction to Multicarbon Products in Near-Neutral KCl Electrolytes
abstract: Reducing CO2 to value-added multicarbon (C2+) fuels and chemicals using renewable energy is a viable way to circumvent CO2 buildup in the atmosphere and facilitate closing the carbon cycle. To date it remains a challenge to achieve high product selectivity and long-term stability of electrocatalytic carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) especially at practically relevant high current levels >100 mA cm−2. Here, we report a simple electrodeposited Cu electrocatalyst on a hydrophobic porous gas-diffusion layer (GDL) electrode affording stable and selective CO2RR to C2+ products in nearneutral KCl electrolytes. By directing the CO2 stream to fully submerged hydrophobic GDLs in a H-cell, high C2+ partial current densities near 100 mA cm−2 were achieved. In a flow-cell setup, the Cu/GDL cathode in 2 M KCl afforded stable CO2RR superior to that in widely used KOH electrolytes. We found that Cu etching/corrosion associated with trace oxygen played a role in the catalyst instability in alkaline media under cathodic CO2RR conditions, a problem largely suppressed in near-neutral electrolyte. A two-electrode CO2 electrolyzer was constructed with a Cu/GDL cathode in KCl catholyte and an anode comprised of nickel−iron hydroxide on nickel foam (NiFe/NF) in a KOH anolyte separated by Nafion membrane. By periodically adding HCl to the KCl catholyte to compensate the increasing pH and remove accumulated (bi)carbonates, we observed little decay over ∼30 h in flow-cell CO2RR activity and selectivity at 150 mA cm−2 with a high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of ∼75% and energy efficiency of 40% for C2+ products.

■ INTRODUCTION The rapid consumption of fossil fuels has caused critical environmental and climate issues. Reducing carbon dioxide (CO2) into fuels and chemical feedstocks using renewable electricity sources could pave the way to a closed carbon cycle.1,2 Great efforts have been devoted to designing various electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). 3−9 Reducing CO2 to carbon monoxide (CO) 10−12 or formate13−15 with Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) > 90% have been achieved; but reducing CO2 beyond the two-electron reduction products, especially the high-value multicarbon (C2+) products such as ethylene (C2H4) and ethanol at high current levels are still challenging and can only be achieved with copper (Cu) and its alloys with moderate selectivity.16−18
Also, long-term stabilities of Cu-based electrocatalysts had been poor due to the presence of various decaying mechanisms,19−21 an issue requiring systematic investigation for developing scalable CO2RR for real-world deployment. 22
A variety of strategies have been developed to enhance the performance of Cu-based electrocatalysts.23−30 In addition to catalyst engineering, electrolytes can also affect their CO2RR performance. It was identified that near-neutral to weakly basic electrolytes were suitable for the formation of C2+ products
due to the optimal balance between favored CO2 transport (in low pH) and suppressed water reduction (in high pH).25,31−35
However, due to the low solubility and low diffusion coefficient of CO2 in aqueous electrolytes,
36 CO2RR current densities were limited to <30 mA cm−2 in conventional H-cell experiments.37 With the implementation of flow cells with gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) for CO2RR, high current densities >100 mA cm−2 could be achieved with the efficient CO2 transport in gas phase to the catalysts (diffusion coefficients of 16 and 0.0016 mm2/s for humidified gaseous CO2 and CO2 in aqueous solution at room temperature, respectively).36,38,39 In addition, highly alkaline potassium hydroxide (KOH) electrolyte in flow-cell experiments, which was not used in conventional H-cell experiments, due to its conversion to KHCO3 by CO2, was found to lower the activation barrier of C−C bond formation and facilitate

production of C2H4. 40 However, electrode degradation over long-term CO2RR was observed, 41 with one of the decay mechanisms being salt precipitation due to the reaction between CO2 and KOH.
42,43 Salt accumulation required refreshing the electrode and electrolyte every several hours,44,45 rendering KOH electrolyte less favorable in longterm operation.22 Additional effort is required to elucidate and understand all possible decay mechanisms of Cu-based electrodes under cathodic CO2RR conditions in KOH, and devise strategies to afford long-term stability of CO2RR at high currents. On the other hand, CO2RR in certain near-neutral electrolytes such as KCl electrolytes have demonstrated high selectivity for producing C2+ products with Cu catalysts.16,46−51 It was reported that Cl− could delay the reduction of electrodeposited cuprous oxide (Cu2O) nanoparticles to generate a biphasic Cu2O−Cu catalyst for selective production of C2−C4 species.46 Cuprous chloride (CuCl) modified Cu mesh in acidic KCl electrolyte achieved ∼60% Faradaic efficiency (FE) for C2H4 at current densities of 50.0−42.1 mA cm−2 at a three-phase interface.52 However, long-term stability with these electrolytes was not investigated. Little has been done on high current CO2RR in near-neutral KCl electrolytes in GDE/flow cell setups,52,53 except for the works on tin (Sn) catalyzed CO2RR to formate,
54−57 possibly due to the change in pH during reaction and larger overpotentials measured in the reversible hydrogen electrode scale compared to that in KOH electrolytes.42
Here, we developed a simple electrodeposition method to prepare Cu electrode directly on commercial carbon-based gasdiffusion layer (GDL) substrates for CO2RR. The Cu/GDL electrodes in potassium chloride (KCl) electrolytes afforded a high FE of 82% and partial current density of 97 mA cm−2 for
C2+ products in H-cells. Directing the CO2 stream to the porous, hydrophobic Cu/GDL electrodes for efficient CO2 transport in the gas phase to the catalysts was found to be a critical factor to achieve such high reaction rates in H-cells. In flow cells, the Cu/GDL cathodes afforded total current densities up to 200 mA cm−2 with a C2+ partial current density of 133 mA cm−2. CO2RR in flow cell with a 2 M KCl catholyte showed good stability superior to that in a 2 M KOH catholyte without compromising activity and selectivity. Cu etching/corrosion during CO2RR in highly alkaline electrolytes was observed possibly promoted by trace oxygen. Cathode corrosion and degradation were greatly suppressed in nearneutral electrolytes to afford much prolonged catalytic stability for CO2RR. Further, a facile approach of adding HCl to the flowing KCl catholyte periodically was devised for maintaining a near-neutral pH and low (bi)carbonate ion concentration to further extend catalyst lifetime for sustained high C2+ production. By doing so in a practically useful two-electrode flow-cell comprised of a Cu/GDL cathode in KCl catholyte and a nickel−iron hydroxides-based anode in KOH anolyte, little decay was observed in the activity and selectivity toward C2+ products at a high current density of 150 mA cm
−2 for ∼30 h, with an energy efficiency of ∼40% (with iR compensation) for C2+ production through CO2RR.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Synthesis and Structural Characterization of the Cu/ GDL Electrode. We simply used commercial porous carbon substrates for Cu electrodeposition to prepare Cu/GDL cathode. The GDL (Sigracet 29 BC) was made of a carbon fiber (CF) backing layer and a hydrophobic microporous layer (MPL). The CF side of GDL was covered by Scotch tape to
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c13427 J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 3245−3255
3246
only expose the MPL side for Cu deposition under −0.3 V vs an Ag/AgCl reference electrode in a 0.15 M CuSO4 + 0.5 M H2SO4 bath for 20 min (Figure 1a for the current density vs time curve and inset for a schematic drawing of the electrode structure). According to the passed charge during electrodeposition, a Cu loading of ∼7.8 mg cm−2 was obtained under this condition (assuming a 100% Faradaic efficiency for Cu deposition). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed that a dense layer of Cu particles with diameters of ∼16 μm were deposited on the substrates (Figure S1a) with rough surface structures observed from the magnified view (Figure S1b). Cross-section image showed the single-layer deposition of Cu particles on the microporous-layer side of the GDL substrate (Figure 1b). X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the Cu/GDL electrodes showed face-centered cubic Cu microcrystals (Figure S2). The Cu/GDL probed by Raman spectroscopy showed peaks at 219 and 632 cm−1 with a shoulder peak at 521 cm−1 (Figure 1c), attributed to the formation of native cuprous oxide (Cu2O) after exposure of Cu to air.58 Elemental mapping confirmed the high purity of deposited Cu particles (Figure 1d), with trace signals of oxygen consistent with the native Cu2O seen in the Raman data (Figure 1c). Impact of CO2 Transport on Electrocatalytic Performance in H-Cell. The CO2RR performance of the Cu/GDL electrode was first investigated in a conventional H-cell. To overcome the poor CO2 transport in aqueous electrolytes (low solubility and diffusion coefficient of CO2),
36 Cu/GDL was immersed in a 2 M KCl electrolyte (with 0.01 M KHCO3 added to buffer pH change during reaction in H-cell, see Figure S3 for details of pH change during reaction) with the CO2 tubing end touching the carbon-fiber side of the electrode substrate to direct the CO2 stream to the backside of electrode. This experimental setup allowed efficient gas-phase CO2 transport through the hydrophobic carbon layer to the Cu electrocatalysts deposited on the microporous layer (configuration 1 in Figure 2a, the default configuration of H-cell experiments in this work). Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) of the Cu/GDL electrodes showed large reduction current densities of ∼110 mA cm−2 at potentials ∼−1.2 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) (Figure S4). For controlled-potential CO2RR under a directed CO2 stream to the cathode in the H-cell at −1.20 V vs RHE for 30 min, we measured a high current density of ∼103 mA cm−2 with impressive 39.9% and 31.1% Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) for C2H4 and ethanol production, respectively (entry 1 in Figure 2b). Control experiments with GDL substrate (subjected to the same preparation procedure as the Cu/ GDL electrode except that the electrodeposition bath was 0.5 M H2SO4 without any Cu precursor) in CO2-saturated electrolyte and Cu/GDL electrode in Ar-saturated electrolyte (without any KHCO3) showed small cathodic current densities of ∼6 and ∼20 mA cm−2 at −1.20 V vs RHE, respectively (Figure S5), much lower than that of ∼103 mA cm−2 with the Cu/GDL electrodes in CO2-saturated electrolyte. Further, H2 was the only product detected in the control experiments, confirming that CO2RR with the Cu catalysts were responsible for the production of carbonaceous products. The electrodeposition parameters, including the concentration of CuSO4 precursor and the deposition time, were varied systematically to reach the optimal synthesis condition discussed above (0.15 M CuSO4 in deposition bath and 20 min deposition time), affording high selectivity and reaction rate for C2+ products
(Figure S6). Strong dependence of product selectivity on particle size was reported for Cu nanoparticle catalysts,59,60 but the optimal Cu catalyst (∼16 μm diameter) and smaller electrodeposited Cu particles (∼2 μm diameter, synthesized with 0.05 M CuSO4 in deposition bath and 10 min deposition time) showed similar product distributions (Figure S7). The total FE reached 77.0% with a partial current density of 79.3 mA cm−2 for C2+ products with the optimal electrodeposited Cu catalyst, while the FE for H2 was only 9.7%. Much of this excellent CO2RR activity was attributed to the markedly enhanced CO2 transport through the hydrophobic carbon layer to the Cu electrocatalysts (1 in Figure 2a). No gas bubble was observed in the electrolyte when the CO2 tubing touched the electrode, indicating that CO2 gas was transported through the GDL to the Cu catalysts and gaseous products released to the headspace of the cathodic compartment through the electrode neck (see Figure S8 for discussion of the impact of electrode neck area). We further performed control experiments to reduce or block gas-phase CO2 transport directed to the Cu catalysts (see configurations 2 and 3 in Figure 2a for modified setups). Directing the CO2 stream into the electrolyte away from the cathode decreased the FE for C2+ products from 77.0% to 61.4% (entry 2 in Figure 2b), which was further deteriorated by covering the electrode neck with epoxy resin
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c13427 J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 3245−3255
3247
(Figure S9 for an image of the epoxy covered electrode) to completely block CO2 from directly reaching the catalyst in the gas-phase (configuration 3 in Figure 2a and entry 3 in Figure 2b). The latter situation was similar to the commonly used Hcell configuration in which the cathode was typically nonporous and/or nonhydrophobic, with dissolved CO2 transporting through the electrolyte being the only CO2 supply to the cathode catalyst for CO2RR (blue dashed arrows in Figure 2a).22 In addition, covering the electrode neck with epoxy but directing the CO2 stream to the backside of the Cu/ GDL electrode showed similar current densities and product selectivity as configuration 1 (Figure S10), indicating sufficient gas-phase CO2 supply from directed CO2 stream. Cu catalysts electrodeposited on substrates without the highly hydrophobic MPL (29BA) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) treatment (29AA) measured with the CO2 stream directed to the substrates showed lower selectivity of CO2RR compared to that on the 29BC substrate (Figure S11), further supporting the critical role of establishing hydrophobic porous network to ensure efficient CO2 transport in gas phase. The enhanced gasphase CO2 transport to the catalysts with the CO2 stream directed to the hydrophobic electrode substrates enabled CO2RR at current densities >100 mA cm
−2 in H-cell experiments, offering a facile platform to investigate the properties and performance of catalysts and electrolytes at conditions close to practical relevant current densities37 before switching to use more complex flow cell setups. Product Selectivity and Electrolyte Engineering in HCell. Potential-dependent product distributions through CO2RR on the Cu/GDL electrodes were investigated with the CO2 stream directed to the carbon-fiber side of the electrodes (configuration 1 in Figure 2a). In 2 M KCl electrolyte, the FE of H2 production decreased from 18.9% to 6.6% under a negative potential shift from −0.95 to −1.15 V, accompanied by decreases in the FEs of the two-electron reduction products of CO and formate. Meanwhile, FEs increased for the more reduced products including C2H4, ethanol, and methane (Figure 3a), with the FE of C2+ products reaching a maximum of 77.0% at −1.20 V. Further negative shift of potential to −1.24 V showed an increase in FE to 23.5% for H2, indicating excessive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at more negative potentials. The product distributions at different applied potentials in terms of moles produced are shown in Figure S12. The amounts of produced CO and formate are relatively insensitive to the applied potential, while the productions of hydrogen, methane, ethylene, and ethanol keep increasing with the cathodic shift of the applied potentials. The partial current densities for C2+ products kept increasing in the potential range of −0.95 to −1.24 V and reached 91.5 mA cm−2 at −1.24 V (Figure 3b). The activity and selectivity toward C2+ products were further enhanced by increasing the KCl concentration to 3 M (slightly under the KCl solubility limit). A high FE of 82.7% and partial current density of 97.3 mA cm−2 for C2+ products were achieved at −1.20 V in a 3 M KCl electrolyte (with added 0.01 M KHCO3 to afford a mild buffering effect, Figure S13). The high C2+ products FE and partial current were impressive considering that a H-cell was used for CO2RR. In another near-neutral 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte (pH = 7.4, see Table S1 for species in the electrolytes) with the same CO2 delivery approach, similar Cu/GDL electrodes also exhibited high activity and selectivity for CO2RR, but with methane as the dominant product with a FE of 39.9% and
partial current density of 33.0 mA cm−2 at −0.90 V vs RHE (Figure S14). Similarly, adding high concentration KHCO3 to the 2 M KCl electrolyte showed negative impact on the C2+ selectivity, exemplified by that the C2+ FE decreased from 77.0% to 61.0% and 25.7% when the initial KHCO3 concentration in the KCl electrolyte increased from 0.01 to 0.1 and 0.5 M, respectively (Figure S15). Although KCl and KHCO3 electrolytes both showed near-neutral pH in equilibrium with CO2 at ambient pressure, their different buffering capabilities resulted in different electrode surface pH under working conditions. The low buffering capability of KCl electrolytes allowed the electrode surface pH to increase to a weakly basic range (pH ∼ 10) before significant reaction between CO2 and OH
− in strongly alkaline conditions as suggested by a “reaction-diffusion” model,61 while the stronger buffering capability of high concentration KHCO3 diminished the surface pH increase. This surface pH increase under cathodic currents in KCl electrolytes benefited C2+ production due to the positive shift of C2+ onset potential with increasing pH,34 in agreement with previous findings at low current densities.16,51 These results demonstrate that aqueous KCl solutions with low buffering capabilities are excellent electrolytes for selective generation of C2+ products at high CO2RR current densities.
CO2RR with near-Neutral KCl and KHCO3 Catholytes in Flow Cell. We next focused on flow-cell experiments with the Cu/GDL electrode as GDE and near-neutral KCl as
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c13427 J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 3245−3255
3248
catholytes for achieving >100 mA cm−2 current densities.36
The experimental setup composed of a gas chamber block, a cathodic block, and an anodic block (Figure 4a). The Cu/GDL CO2RR cathode was paired with an efficient nickel−iron hydroxides on nickel foam (NiFe/NF) anode for oxygen evolution reaction (OER),62 separated by a Nafion membrane to prevent the crossover of liquid products from CO2RR. Two M KCl presaturated with argon (Ar) and 2 M KOH were circulated with peristaltic pumps as the catholyte and anolyte for CO2RR and OER, respectively (Figure 4b). The blocked Cl− transport from the KCl catholyte to the KOH anolyte by the Nafion cation-exchange membrane and the suppressed chlorine evolution compared to oxygen evolution in highly alkaline anolytes synergistically prevented chlorine-induced corrosion of the NiFe/NF anode.63
Prior to two-electrode CO2RR electrolyzer operation, a cathodic block equipped with an Ag/AgCl reference electrode was used for three-electrode measurements. Controlled-current electrolysis was conducted with the flow cell in the current density range of 100 to 200 mA cm−2. Stable CO2RR activities were observed for 70 min in this current density range with the Cu/GDL cathode in 2 M KCl catholyte (Figure 4c). Product distributions showed that selectivity was almost the same when increasing current densities from 100 to 150 mA cm−2. The
FEs were ∼41% and ∼30% for C2H4 and ethanol respectively (Figure 4d). The CO2RR selectivity on Cu/GDL in flow cell at 100 mA cm−2 was close to that in H cell at similar current densities (−1.20 V in Figure 3a), consistent with the efficient delivery of CO2 to the cathode through the gas phase by directing the CO2 stream in H-cell. The higher total current density of 150 mA cm−2 in the flow cell led to increased partial current density for C2+ products to 120.6 mA cm
−2 (Figure 4e). When the current density increased to 200 mA cm−2, FEs of H2 and methane increased together with a decrease in the FE of C2H4 (Figure 4d) due to activation of a methane production pathway at larger overpotentials.64 Nevertheless, the partial current densities for C2+ products increased to 133.4 mA cm−2 (Figure 4e). Furthermore, the Cu/GDL electrodes were tested in near-
neutral 2 M KHCO3 catholytes. The stronger buffering capability of 2 M KHCO3 catholyte and lower electrode surface pH under cathodic currents compared to 2 M KCl catholyte caused higher FEs of 34.2% for H2 and lower FE of 42.7% for C2+ products at 150 mA cm
−2 (Figure S16), consistent with the unfavorable generation of C2+ products using a higher concentration 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte from H-cell experiments (Figure S14).

Comparison of KCl and KOH Catholytes in TwoElectrode Flow Cells for CO2RR. The performance of the Cu/GDL cathode in KCl catholyte was compared to that with the Cu/GDL cathode in commonly used KOH catholyte40,66 in two-electrode CO2 electrolyzers. In both cases, NiFe/NF was used as the OER anode with 2 M KOH anolyte to reduce the overpotential of the anode side. K+ was the major charge carrier transporting from the anolyte to the catholyte across the Nafion cation-exchange membrane to balance the charge during electrochemical reactions (see the Supplementary Methods in the Supporting Information for discussions of mass transport in the CO2RR electrolyzer). The Cu/GDL electrode in 2 M KCl catholyte showed higher selectivity of reducing CO2 to C2+ products (FE ∼ 80.4%) than in 2 M KOH catholyte (FE ∼ 67.2%) under controlled-current electrolysis for 70 min at the current density of 150 mA cm−2 (Figures 5 a and S17). The CO2 electrolyzer with 2 M KOH catholyte exhibited lower cell voltages compared to that with 2 M KCl catholyte (Figure 5b), due to the higher ionic conductivity of KOH catholyte (cell resistance measured to be ∼7.2 and 5.8 Ω with KCl and KOH catholytes, respectively). However, after iR compensation, the cell voltages of the CO2RR electrolyzers composed of the NiFe/NF anode in 2 M KOH anolyte and Cu/GDL cathode in 2 M KCl or 2 M KOH catholytes operated at 150 mA cm−2 were both ∼2.2 V, and a high C2+ FE of ∼80.4% was only obtained with the KCl catholyte. The similar activities of Cu/GDL in KCl and KOH
catholytes independent of pH were consistent with the CO2RR mechanism that the rate-determining C−C bond formation step does not involve proton transfer, and the working potential to achieve similar activities was independent of pH on the standard hydrogen electrode scale.67
In addition to the better selectivity of CO2RR to C2+ products in the KCl catholyte, the Cu/GDL cathodes showed superior operation stability in the KCl catholyte than in the KOH catholyte. For CO2RR in KOH catholyte operated at 150 mA cm−2, the FE of C2H4 decreased quickly from 36.8% to 14.2% in 3 h, accompanied by an increase in FE of H2 from 13.8% to 34.1% (Figure 5c). Fast decay of C2+ selectivity within ∼2 h using Cu catalysts on commercial carbon-based GDL substrates in KOH catholytes was also observed previously.40 In contrast, the FEs of C2H4 and H2 were stable in the same duration for CO2RR at 150 mA cm
−2 in KCl catholyte (Figure 5c). Although surface restructure of Cu particles at the nanoscale was observed after reacting in KCl catholyte (Figure S18),27,68 the stable FEs of C2H4 indicated the relative insensitivity of products selectivity to surface restructure of large, tens of microns sized Cu particles.60 CO2 gas across the Cu/GDL cathodes into catholytes at ∼1 mL min−1 was observed during operation, which would be converted to carbonate ions reacting with the KOH catholyte. However, the carbonate concentration due to the CO2 leakage after the 3 h reaction would be ∼0.02 M, and the pH of the 2 M KOH catholyte was still measured to be >14. Hence, the
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c13427 J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 3245−3255
3250
quickly decaying C2+ selectivity with KOH catholyte should reflect the intrinsic properties of the dominant KOH species. SEM image of the Cu/GDL electrodes showed loss of Cu catalysts after CO2RR in the KOH catholyte (Figure S19a), which was further corroborated by decreases in the Cu 2p and Cu LMM signals (at binding energy ∼933 and 568 eV, respectively) from X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of the reacted electrode compared to a freshly made electrode (Figure S20). No obvious damage to the dense layer of Cu particles was seen on the electrode after CO2RR in the KCl catholyte for the same time of 3 h (Figure S19b). The KOH and KCl catholytes before and after reaction were subjected to inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) measurements (Table S2). The Cu concentration increased considerably from 12.4 to 302.3 parts per billion (ppb) after electrolysis in the KOH catholyte, consistent with the loss of the Cu catalysts into the KOH catholyte. Although the Cu concentration increased from below the detection limit (∼2 ppb) to 14.1 ppb after electrolysis in the KCl catholyte, this was much lower than that in the KOH catholyte, consistent with the higher stability of Cu/GDL in the KCl catholyte (Figure 5c). We suggest that the Cu catalyst and the native Cu2O on the surface were prone to corrosion even under cathodic CO2RR potentials,27,69−71 which could be further promoted by oxidizing intermediates or trace O2 inevitably existing in the electrolytes and flow cell. Intentionally increasing the O2 level in the 2 M KOH catholyte by air bubbling (O2 levels measured to be 0.2 ± 0.3 and 3.7 ± 0.6 mg L−1 in Ar- and air-saturated KOH catholytes respectively, see Table S2 for details) led to faster decay of CO2RR selectivity and higher Cu concentration (392.8 ppb) in catholyte than in the Ar-saturated KOH catholyte (Figure S21), indicating the plausible role of oxidative etching in Cu catalyst corrosion and deactivation. Similar trend was observed by bubbling air into the 2 M KCl catholyte (Figure S22), but the performance decay was still much slower than that in KOH catholyte (Figure 5c). According to the Pourbaix diagram of Cu,72 Cu could be oxidized to Cu(OH)4
2− more easily in highly alkaline KOH catholytes than in the near-neutral KCl catholytes, consistent with the observed enhanced stability of Cu/GDL in KCl catholytes than in KOH catholytes (Figure 5c). Magnified cross-section SEM image at the Cu-GDL interface showed the partial contact of Cu particles with the carbon-based substrate (Figure S23). Although we observed that the Cu particles could withstand sonicating in ethanol, it might be possible that corrosion of Cu at the catalyst-substrate interface could weaken the adhesion of Cu particles to the GDL substrates to induce particle falling-off, which could be another pathway for Cu loss (Figure S19a). Periodic Addition of HCl to KCl Catholyte in TwoElectrode Flow Cells for CO2RR. Decay of CO2RR selectivity was also observed in prolonged operation in KCl with the FE of ethylene decreased from 40.6% to 29.9% and FE of H2 increased from 10.7% to 21.7% at 20 h (Figure 5d). The electron- and proton-transfer processes involved in CO2RR left OH
− in the KCl catholyte, which would be further converted to (bi)carbonates by reacting with the small amount of CO2 across the Cu/GDL cathode. By measuring the catholyte pH and the total amount of (bi)carbonates in the KCl catholytes (measured by titration with acid), the concentration of bicarbonate and carbonate ions in KCl catholytes could be obtained after long-term CO2RR (see the
Supplementary Methods in the Supporting Information for details). Bicarbonate (35 mM) and carbonate (63 mM) with pH increasing to 10.6 were observed in the KCl catholytes after reacting for 12 h (Table S3). The accumulated (bi)carbonates in KCl catholytes could cause the decay in long-term CO2RR, as observed from the low C2+ and high H2 selectivity in KHCO3 catholytes (Figure S16).
16 Another explanation for the decay of CO2RR performance could be the increased pH of KCl catholytes and associated faster Cu etching in alkaline conditions. The accumulated (bi)carbonates in the KCl catholytes and the increased catholyte pH could simultaneously lead to the gradually decrease of C2+ FE in prolonged operation. We found that the gradual decay of C2+ FE in long-term operation with KCl catholytes could be alleviated by neutralization with HCl (release of CO2 gas bubbles with the addition of HCl to the catholyte was observed). Automated/programmed addition of 2.7 mL of a 2.13 M HCl solution every hour to the KCl catholyte (tuned to match the generation rate of OH− from CO2RR, ∼5.6 mmol per hour at a total current of 150 mA) was carried out during electrolysis to maintain catholyte pH ∼7.0, affording further improved stability of the Cu/GDL electrodes in KCl catholyte. Otherwise, pH of the KCl catholyte would increase to 10.6 after 12 h reaction without HCl addition (Table S3). Little decay of C2H4 selectivity was observed for ∼30 h with HCl addition at a current density of 150 mA cm−2 (Figure 5d and S24), superior to the case without the automated addition of HCl. Nevertheless, we did observe failure of Cu/GDL cathode in KCl catholyte with a sharp decrease of C2+ selectivity and increase of H2 selectivity (Figure S25) after 30 h. A recent work on silver catalysts with KOH catholyte in a GDE setup reported similar sharp decrease of CO2RR selectivity, which matched a sharp increase of electrochemical capacitance of the Ag/GDL electrode.43 Thus, the origin of the Ag/GDL electrode failure was attributed to electrode flooding. Electrode flooding by electrolyte would fill the porous network to block gas-phase CO2 transport and deteriorate the CO2RR performance, which might also explain the sharp decrease of C2+ selectivity of Cu/GDL cathodes in KCl catholyte. The electrodeposited Cu cathode in 2 M KCl catholyte
paired with a NiFe/NF anode in 2 M KOH anolyte exhibited stable CO2RR for 30 h at 150 mA cm
−2. High overall FE of 75.1% and full-cell energy conversion efficiency (ECE, defined as the ratio between stored chemical energy and input electric energy) of 40% (with iR compensation, 27% before iR compensation, see Supplementary Methods in the SI for details) for C2+ products were obtained with the 30 h operation, indicating the advantages of KCl catholyte for Cu catalysts. To the best of our knowledge, Cu catalysts with KCl catholytes in GDE/flow cell setups have not been characterized at high current densities (>100 mA cm−2). Compared to previous reports of Cu-based catalysts in KOH catholytes, the employment of KCl catholytes and automatic addition of HCl during reaction presented an important strategy to achieve high C2+ selectivity and stability (see Table S4 for comparison with previous reports). A solution-synthesized Cu nanocatalyst paired with an iridium oxide (IrOx) anode afforded 4 h of CO2RR at 150 mA cm
−2 in 1 M KOH electrolyte with FE of ∼26% and ECE of ∼14% (without iR compensation) for C2+ products.
38 An additive-controlled, electrodeposited nanoporous Cu catalysts was measured with a flow cell setup in 1 M KOH electrolyte and FEs of 38.2% and
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c13427 J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 3245−3255
3251
25.4% for ethylene and ethanol, respectively, were reported at current densities ∼190 mA cm−2.39 The high C2+ selectivity was attributed to the promotion of C1 intermediate dimerization on the rich steps and edges presented on the nanoporous surface, but long-term operation was not reported in that system. A graphite-stabilized sputtered Cu on hydrophobic PTFE electrode paired with a nickel−iron oxides (NiFeOx) anode demonstrated full-cell operation at ∼110 mA cm−2 in 7 M KOH electrolyte for ∼1 h with an ECE of 34% (without iR compensation) for ethylene.40 Recently, the sputtered Cu on PTFE electrode was modified with a COproducing iron porphyrin catalyst and paired with an IrOx anode in a membrane-electrode assembly device (the CO2RR cathode was in direct contact with an anion-exchange membrane, so no catholyte was used in such system) to afford 12 h operation with decaying current densities from 120 to 110 mA cm−2 and ∼73% FE and ∼23% ECE (without iR compensation) for C2+ products.
73 Overall, the high C2+ selectivity, activity, stability of our Cu/GDL electrode in near-neutral and nonbuffering KCl catholyte with automatic HCl neutralization to remove accumulated (bi)carbonates and maintain near-neutral pH represent a promising strategy for CO2RR to valuable C2+ fuels and chemicals.
■ CONCLUSIONS We developed a facile electro-position method to synthesize Cu catalysts directly on commercial GDL, exhibiting excellent selectivity for CO2RR to C2+ products in KCl electrolytes with FEs of 82.7% and 80.4% at current densities >100 mA cm−2 in H-cell and flow cell setups, respectively. The high current densities achieved in H-cell setups enabled by efficient gasphase CO2 transport to the Cu catalysts could markedly improve the efficiency of catalyst evaluation at practically relevant current densities. When paired with a NiFe/NF anode and KOH anolyte in flow cell, the Cu/GDL cathodes can be stably operated at a current density of 150 mA cm−2 for ∼30 h in the KCl catholyte with automated HCl addition to neutralize the accumulated (bi)carbonates. The use of nearneutral KCl catholytes enhanced catalyst lifetime by avoiding the severe etching and loss of Cu catalysts in commonly used highly alkaline KOH catholytes. The excellent stability of Cu catalysts in KCl electrolytes without compromises of selectivity and activity for CO2RR to C2+ products offered a great choice of catholyte to enhance the economic viability of CO2RR electrolyzers.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Synthesis of Cu/GDL. All electrochemical measurements were conducted with a CHI 760D potentiostat. For electrodes in H cell experiments, the carbon fiber (CF) side of a commercial gas-diffusion layer (GDL, Sigracet 29 BC, 3 × 1 cm2) was covered by Scotch tape to ensure solely exposure of the microporous layer (MPL) for deposition. The Cu deposition bath was composed of 0.15 M CuSO4 (99.999% trace metals basis, Sigma) and 0.5 M H2SO4 (Certified ACS Plus, Fisher). The GDL was used as working electrode with an Ag/ AgCl (filled with saturated KCl) reference electrode and a high-purity Cu wire (99.999% trace metals basis, diameter 2.0 mm, Sigma) counter electrode. The GDL substrate was held at −0.3 V vs reference electrode for 20 min with gentle stirring of the electrolyte. The Scotch tape was removed after electrodeposition and the Cu/GDL electrode was dried in vacuum at room temperature. For Cu/GDL electrodes in flow cell experiments, the GDL substrates were cut into 4 × 1.2 cm2 for Cu electrodeposition. For Cu/GDL electrodes tested with CO2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolytes in H cell, the deposition bath
was changed to 0.05 M CuSO4 + 0.5 M H2SO4 and the GDL substrate was held at −0.25 V vs reference electrode for 10 min.
Preparation of NiFe/NF Anode. The nickel−iron hydroxides on nickel foam (NiFe/NF) anode were prepared by a previously reported electrodeposition method with minor modifications.62 Commercial Ni foams (4 × 1 cm2) were sonicated in acetone for 3 min and dried at ambient environment. The deposition bath was composed of 18 mM Ni(NO3)2 and 6 mM Fe(NO3)3. The Ni foam was used as working electrode with an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a Pt mesh counter electrode, which was held at −1.0 V vs reference electrode for 10 min without stirring. A Ni tab current collector was attached to the NiFe/ NF anode and covered by epoxy resin to define an active area of 1 × 1 cm2 for flow cell experiments.
Material Characterizations. The size and morphology of the prepared samples were characterized using a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Hitachi S-4800) operating at 15 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained with Rigaku Miniflex using Cu Kα radiation. Raman spectroscopy was conducted on a Horiba Raman spectrometer equipped with an Olympus BX41 microscope and a Spectra-Physics 532 nm Ar laser. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out with a PHI 5000 VersaProbe system with an Al Kα (1486.6 eV) radiation source. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) measurements were performed using a Thermo Scientific XSERIES 2 ICP-MS equipment.
CO2RR in H Cell Setup. The electrochemical setup involved a gastight two-compartment H cell separated by a Nafion 117 cationexchange membrane. Two M KCl (for molecular biology, ≥99.0%, Sigma) + 0.01 M KHCO3 (99.7%, Sigma) solution was used as catholytes (30 mL of catholyte with ∼20 mL headspace) with stirring. A high-purity CO2 (99.999%, Praxair) stream at 20 standard cubic centimeters per minute (sccm) was delivered into the cathodic compartment for 20 min prior to measurements. The Cu/GDL electrode (active area of 1 × 1 cm2) was used as the working electrode with the 20 sccm CO2 stream directed to the carbon fiber side of the electrode during reaction. An Ag/AgCl electrode was placed in the cathodic chamber as the reference electrode. One M K2CO3 (ACS, ≥ 99%, Sigma) solution (30 mL) was used as anolyte with a graphite rod as counter electrode. The electrode was prescanned by linear sweep voltametry (LSV) from −0.5 V vs the reference electrode to the desired potentials for controlled-potential electrolysis at 50 mV/s before constant-potential electrolysis. All potentials were recorded against the Ag/AgCl reference electrode and converted to vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) with iR compensations by the following equation

removal as shown in Figure 4a. Special attention should be paid to the cleanness of the PTFE cell blocks (sonicated in 6 M nitric acid and boiled in deionized water before use) and silicone gaskets (wiped with ethanol and boiled in deionized water before use) to ensure the reproducibility. The electrodeposited Cu/GDL cathode was affixed on a silicone gasket (with Cu tape on all four sides) with a window of 2 × 0.5 cm2 to define the electrode active area. Another piece of Cu tape was attached to the electrode as the current collecter. A NiFe/ NF anode (active area of 1 × 1 cm2) was used as the counter electrode. A cathodic block with a port to insert an Ag/AgCl reference electrode was used for three-electrode experiments. The cathodic and anodic blocks were separated by a Nafion 117 memebrane. For shortterm experiments, 100 mL of Ar-saturated 2 M KCl (or 2 M KOH/ KHCO3) catholyte was flowed through the cathodic block and circulated by a peristaltic pump at a flow rate of 5 mL min−1. A 100 mL portion of 2 M KOH (ACS, ≥ 85%, Sigma) anolyte was flowed through the anodic block and circulated by another peristaltic pump. All electrolytes used in flow cell experiments were purified by Chelex 100 resins (Bio-Rad, regenerated with 1 M HCl and 1 M KOH) to remove impurity cations. The assembled flow cell was operated in constant-current mode for 70 min with GC sampled at 15, 38, and 61 min to represent the average gaseous production rate. The product quantification protocols were the same as the H cell experiments. For long-term experiments without automated acid addition, the volumes of the catholyte and anolyte were increased to 400 and 200 mL, respectively, and the GC sample interval was set to 30 min. For longterm experiments with automated HCl addition, 2.7 mL of a 2.13 M HCl (ACS reagent, 37%, Sigma) solution was added to the catholyte reservoir (150 mL Ar-saturated 2 M KCl catholyte with stirring) every hour by a dosing pump (Jebao) during electrolysis. C-Flex tubes (Sigma) were used for all liquid transfer processes to avoid introduction of impurities.
